Opening

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 4 · LESSON A · 2 MINUTES

Follow the Warming Chain · Classic

Learning objective

I can explain how extra greenhouse gases affect warming, then plan a safe action and a useful way to check it.

Success looks like

  • Link a human activity to greenhouse gases and warming.
  • Distinguish weather, climate, mitigation and adaptation.
  • Use comparable before/after evidence without overstating what it proves.

A self-contained 40-minute Classic alternative: follow the cause, explain an effect, then complete one evidence-based Record A with a useful action.

One 40-minute Classic alternative

Use this self-contained lesson instead of the paired version where appropriate. It is not an extra compulsory week.

Point, speak, sign, move cards, draw, write or direct an adult. Choose one route; equivalent science evidence does not require a written conversion.

Burning oil or coal adds which greenhouse gas?

I do

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 4 · LESSON A · 7 MINUTES

Watch, predict, explain

Predict, model, explain

Activity → extra greenhouse gases → changed energy balance → warming → an effect. Match an action to its mechanism.

Make a prediction. Change one view, then use a label to explain what you notice.

Sunlight warms the surface. Earth emits infrared; some energy escapes to space.

Worked explanation · reveal after thinking

Greenhouse gases absorb and emit infrared in different directions; energy still escapes to space. Extra greenhouse gases initially reduce outgoing energy at a given temperature; warming moves towards a new balance. This is not a sealed lid. One cold day neither proves nor disproves a long-term global trend. Land ice, not a floating ice cube analogy, is used for sea-level effects.

Local explainer · 32 seconds · silent with captions

Use instead of part of the demonstration. It never autoplays and needs no internet.

Full text / no-video alternative

00–08 seconds · Energy moves
Sunlight warms the surface. Earth emits infrared; some energy escapes to space.

08–16 seconds · Extra greenhouse gases
More greenhouse gases can initially reduce net energy loss, so the climate system warms.

16–24 seconds · Follow a cause chain
Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide. Warming can melt land ice and raise sea level.

24–32 seconds · Choose and check an action
Mitigation addresses causes; adaptation reduces harm. A before/after check needs comparable conditions.

We do

GROW · SCIENCE · Autumn 2 · Week 4 · LESSON A · 10 MINUTES

Match a scenario to a useful science action

Choose a card, read its evidence, then place it in a group. Explain one decision together.

Drag, or select a card and press a group button. Tab and Enter work too; an adult can follow your pointing.

Addresses a cause

Reduces harm from an impact

Unsupported claim

Choose a card first. No cards have been placed.

Read the card clues

Unused lights: An adult-authorised reduction in unnecessary electricity use can reduce generation demand.

Safe shade plan: A suitable shade plan can reduce heat exposure.

Insulate appropriately: Building improvements can reduce energy needed for heating, subject to safe ventilation and professional design.

Heat safety check: Adults adjust a safe activity plan during heat; this reduces exposure rather than removing greenhouse gases.

Poster proves cooling: A poster count is not a measurement of emissions or global temperature.

One cold day disproves warming: One local day is not a long-term global pattern.

Would a small change help? · optional

You may ask for a clearer diagram, fewer cards at once, reading help or more thinking time. Tell your teacher, ask privately, point or pass. Your teacher will say what can change and check whether it helped. No extra sheet is needed.

Two small checks

Supported · 2 questions

1. Chain

Place “extra carbon dioxide” before or after “burn fossil fuel”.

Help beside the question
A cause adds the gas.

Answer guidance

Answer: After burn fossil fuel.

2. Action and limit

Name a useful action and what one local check cannot prove.

Help beside the question
Point, choose or say. Match an action to its mechanism.

Answer guidance

Answer: An authorised reduction in unnecessary electricity use can reduce demand; a local use count does not prove the whole planet cooled.

Standard · 2 questions

1. Chain

Give one cause → process → effect explanation.

Help beside the question
Burning fuel → extra greenhouse gas → warming → an effect.

Answer guidance

Answer: Burning fossil fuel adds CO2, altering net infrared loss and leading to warming; warming can melt land ice.

2. Action and limit

Name a useful action and what one local check cannot prove.

Help beside the question
Match an action to its mechanism.

Answer guidance

Answer: An authorised reduction in unnecessary electricity use can reduce demand; a local use count does not prove the whole planet cooled.

Stretch · 2 questions

1. Chain

Give one cause → process → effect explanation.

Help beside the question
Use an accurate science word. Burning fuel → extra greenhouse gas → warming → an effect.

Answer guidance

Answer: Burning fossil fuel adds CO2, altering net infrared loss and leading to warming; warming can melt land ice.

2. Action and limit

Compare a mitigation action with an adaptation action in one sentence.

Help beside the question
Causes versus harm.

Answer guidance

Answer: Reducing emissions targets the cause; a safe shade plan reduces heat exposure without itself removing the cause.

Knowledge organiser

GROW Science · Autumn 2 · Week 4 · Shared resource · Shared resource

Learning objective

I can explain how extra greenhouse gases affect warming, then plan a safe action and a useful way to check it.

Key words

climate — patterns of weather over many years

greenhouse gas — gas that absorbs and emits infrared radiation

mitigation — limiting warming by addressing its causes

adaptation — adjusting to reduce harm from impacts

baseline — measurement before a change

Remember

  • The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warmer than it would otherwise be.
  • Burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide.
  • Extra greenhouse gases initially reduce energy loss to space, leading to warming.
  • A local action check is not a measurement of global temperature change.

Success looks like

  • Link a human activity to greenhouse gases and warming.
  • Distinguish weather, climate, mitigation and adaptation.
  • Use comparable before/after evidence without overstating what it proves.

Activity → extra greenhouse gases → changed energy balance → warming → an effect. Match an action to its mechanism.

Word help

climate
patterns of weather over many years
greenhouse gas
gas that absorbs and emits infrared radiation
mitigation
limiting warming by addressing its causes
adaptation
adjusting to reduce harm from impacts
baseline
measurement before a change

TA Brief

Current stage

Current stage:

Preparation and access

Use diagrams, clean cards and fictional examples. No family carbon data, spending or pledges are required. Only adults authorise changes to school equipment. Never switch off safety lighting, necessary heating, ventilation, fridges or medical equipment.

Scientific care

Greenhouse gases absorb and emit infrared in different directions; energy still escapes to space. Extra greenhouse gases initially reduce outgoing energy at a given temperature; warming moves towards a new balance. This is not a sealed lid. One cold day neither proves nor disproves a long-term global trend. Land ice, not a floating ice cube analogy, is used for sea-level effects.

Responsive feedback within teaching

The lesson teacher hears an optional request, explains what can change, tries it and checks the effect. Passing or asking privately is valid. No compulsory participation task or new pupil form. Do not infer assessment codes from a click, download or written box.

Sources and scope

  • NASA · Causes of climate change
  • Met Office · Causes of climate change

Audience and response

The lesson teacher is the named adult audience. Hear or read the pupil’s own science response. A click, downloaded file or completed box is not evidence that a request was heard.

Respond within the existing task

Offer reading help, fewer cards at once, clearer labels, an adult-directed model or additional thinking time. Say what can and cannot change, then check whether the adjustment helped.

No additional pupil artefact

A response can be spoken, pointed, signed, drawn or written. Do not require a separate Lundy record, signature or written conversion of an oral response.

An optional pupil-owned note such as “What I said, and what it changed” may be used in existing work. It is not a requirement. If scribing, keep the pupil’s own words; the adult is an audience, not a verifier.

Keep assessment honest

Use current school recording practice and unit criteria separately. This pack does not certify an award. Do not infer a policy code from automated checking or a download.
